title.analysis: Authentic title "The Crypto Trap That Keeps The Middle Class Poor" promises a structural argument that crypto extracts wealth from middle-income buyers. The script delivers that argument (timing, fees, taxes, influencers, collapses, regulation) and then concedes a small regulated ETF allocation can be reasonable. The title matches, though "trap" is stronger than the balanced close.

script.stored_text_completeness: All 19896 canonical characters read sequentially in full in 1 bounded ranges; auto-generated untimed text; stored text ends on the closing line ("They're the ones selling it to you.") with no sign-off; ASR artifacts ("Dauan", "Safeoon", "bare market", "Cury.", "[snorts]", "Black Rockck"); composite Marcus; audio, timed delivery and editing unverified.
script.opening_words: It's 100 a.m. and you're on your phone in the bathroom so your wife doesn't see you. You're reading about some 19-year-old who claims he turned his stimulus check into a Lamborghini trading Dogecoin. And you're sitting there with $6,300 in checking, mortgage due in 8 days. Your kid needs braces and your 2014 Civic's check engine light has been on so long you've named it Gerald. You're thinking, "Am I the only person not getting rich?" Meet Marcus. He's
script.ending_words: That's how you avoid becoming another Marcus lying to your spouse about where the down payment went. That's how you avoid becoming another statistic in someone else's research paper about the true cost of crypto. Be boring. Get rich slowly. Um, actually sleep at night instead of checking Coinbase at 3:00 a.m. The people getting rich off crypto aren't the ones buying it. They're the ones selling it to you.
script.analysis: Full 19896 canonical characters read. A single-narrator long-form essay built around composite Marcus: 1 a.m. FOMO hook, BIS loss statistics, income distribution of holders, Super Bowl ads and influencers, FOMO psychology and timing, fees, opportunity cost, wage-productivity stagnation, financial literacy, taxes, exchange revenue, the 2022 collapses, institutional advantages, ETFs and volatility, scams and meme coins, lobbying and enforcement, genuine uses, wealthy-investor allocation, and a "be boring" close. Several calculations are internally inconsistent (S&P 45% in a falling year, fee totals, Marcus's two counterfactuals) and the story has timeline contradictions.

claim_audit.claim: A BIS study across 95 countries found 73%-81% of crypto investors lose money; average loss $431, about 48% of what was invested.

claim_audit.assessment: Partly verified: BIS Bulletin 69 (Feb 2023) finds most retail app users in nearly all economies lost money on bitcoin from Aug 2015 to Dec 2022 (BIS1). The 73-81% range and the $431 (about 48%) loss match the bulletin by analyst recall; the $431 figure is a median, not an average. The script turns a historical estimate into a forecast about viewers ('will lose money'). MISLEADING framing.
